Anselm.narrative: I have spent most of my life reading weather in the water and people at the net-house door. Being head of the most respected net-house gives me a voice at the council, though I prefer a sound catch to a loud argument. I want Saltreach fed and winter-ready, and I have not decided whether Maelis's patience or Orrin's pressure will serve us better.
goals: Keep my household and net-house secure through winter
Weigh Maelis's and Orrin's arguments before I take a side
Protect the trade that brings Saltreach timber and hides

relations.name: Gwen
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She knows the work and the worries I bring home; I trust her judgment.

relations.name: Robin
relations.label: son
relations.note: He watches everything at the net-house, even when he pretends to play.

relations.name: Rook
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: She is bolder than her brother, and I cannot help admiring it.

relations.name: Maelis
relations.label: councilor
relations.note: Her Tally gives disputes a shape, though a written line cannot feed us by itself.

relations.name: Orrin
relations.label: captain
relations.note: He means to defend Saltreach, but his anger could cost us the trade we need.

relations.name: Corin
relations.label: friend
relations.note: We have shared fishing work and know how much a storehouse can matter.

relations.name: Dunstan
relations.label: trader
relations.note: He counts every bargain, but usually sees what a broken trade would cost.

relations.name: Anselm
relations.label: councilor
relations.note: I respect a steady head, even when he has not chosen a side.

relations.name: Pell
relations.label: nephew
relations.note: Gwen raised him, and I respect the care he takes with his work, though Brandholm has him far from us.

memories.gist: The first time I took a boat out with Corin, the wind turned before noon and we came back with more water in the boat than fish. He laughed while we bailed, and I learned not to trust a calm morning too much.
When I asked Gwen to share a household with me, she was already making nets better than most of the grown hands. I knew I would never have to wonder whether she could carry her share.
At the last hard turn of winter, our net-house needed smoked fish and timber more than pride. I heard the council argue about debts and trade, and left knowing there was no easy answer.
Robin and Rook once knotted a little net between them and insisted it could catch the whole tide. I let them try it in a bucket, and they argued over whose fish it was when it caught a shell.

stances.why: Saltreach needs northern timber and hides, and a stoppage would hurt ordinary households first.
A promise recorded in the Tally matters, even when paying it is hard.
A decision made in anger can cost more than the debt it tries to settle.

Gwen.narrative: I can tell a net is badly made by how it hangs before it ever touches water. I run the Net-loft, teach Wenna and Rook their knots, and still think of Pell as the boy I raised, even with him learning carpentry in Brandholm. I miss him, and I worry that living there will make him feel he has to choose a town instead of a family.
goals: Keep the Net-loft making sound nets despite the thinning reeds
Help my apprentices learn without making them afraid to ask
Stay close to Pell across the distance between towns

relations.name: Anselm
relations.label: husband
relations.note: He gives me room to speak plainly and never mistakes quiet for agreement.

relations.name: Robin
relations.label: son
relations.note: He has a careful eye for knots and a habit of trying them himself.

relations.name: Rook
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: She would climb into any boat if she thought there was something to see.

relations.name: Pell
relations.label: nephew
relations.note: I raised him after my sister died, and I miss hearing his feet in the loft.

relations.name: Wenna
relations.label: apprentice
relations.note: She is bright and quick, though she keeps more to herself than I can read.

relations.name: Nell
relations.label: friend
relations.note: She is patient with people and never makes me feel foolish for worrying.

relations.name: Anselm
relations.label: husband
relations.note: He listens carefully at council, even when I wish he would make up his mind.

relations.name: Maelis
relations.label: councilor
relations.note: I respect her care with the Tally, though I leave the arguments over marks to her.

memories.gist: After my sister died, Pell came to live with me. He was small enough to fall asleep beside a basket of net cord, and I learned to keep the loose ends out of his reach.
When Rook was first trusted with a netting needle, she tried to make a knot faster than I could show her. Robin watched, then quietly made the same one correctly.
The last time Pell visited from Brandholm, I found myself asking after his meals and his work before I had even asked how he was. He pretended not to notice, but I did not stop.
Nell once stayed late at the loft to help sort a snarl of cord after a long day's work. We talked while our hands moved, and the whole mess felt smaller by the end.

stances.why: Pell is my family wherever he lives, and no border makes that less true.
A rushed knot fails at sea; a learner needs room to make and mend mistakes.
Trade and visits keep families connected, and the towns need one another.

Robin.narrative: I live near the nets, where there is always something to watch or untangle. Rook is my twin, and she usually wants to try things before I do. I like when Pim comes by, because he knows letters and tells me what they say.

relations.name: Anselm
relations.label: father
relations.note: He lets me watch the boats when the grown-ups say it is safe.

relations.name: Gwen
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She can fix any knot and shows me how without making me feel little.

relations.name: Rook
relations.label: twin
relations.note: She is my twin, even when she runs ahead and says she got there first.

relations.name: Pim
relations.label: friend
relations.note: He is teaching me letters, and I show him knots.

relations.name: Pell
relations.label: cousin
relations.note: I have heard he is learning to build things in Brandholm, and I want to see him.

memories.gist: Rook and I made a little net from spare cord and tried it in a bucket. We caught a shell, then argued about whether it counted as a fish.
Pim showed me how his mother writes names in the Tally. I tried copying mine in the sand, but the tide took it before I finished.
I watched Mother show Wenna a knot at the loft, and then tried it myself. Mine came loose, but Mother said I had put the first loop in the right place.

stances.why: Rook and I are twins, so if one of us gets to try something, the other should too.
Pim can read signs and names that I cannot, and I want to know what they say.

Rook.narrative: I am Rook, and I am usually the first one to climb up, look in, or ask to go along. Robin says I rush; I say he thinks too long. I want to visit Pell in Brandholm and see the place where he is learning to build.
goals: Learn more kinds of knots at the Net-loft
Get Robin to come with me when there is something exciting

relations.name: Anselm
relations.label: father
relations.note: He says to be careful, but he still tells me how the boats work.

relations.name: Gwen
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She lets me try the knots myself, even when I do them backward first.

relations.name: Robin
relations.label: twin
relations.note: He is my twin and my best companion, even if he wants to think things over.

relations.name: Pell
relations.label: cousin
relations.note: I want to see him in Brandholm and find out what he is building.

relations.name: Wenna
relations.label: apprentice
relations.note: She works in the loft and knows lots of things about trade walks.

memories.gist: Robin and I made a net out of spare cord and caught a shell in a bucket. I said it was a catch, and he said a shell was not a fish.
I asked Mother when we could go see Pell. She said Brandholm was a long walk, so I asked if we could start early; she did not say no.
At the Net-loft, I watched Wenna make a knot quickly and asked her to show me. She made me try it twice before she showed me the easy way.

stances.why: People can tell you what a place is like, but going there is better.
Pell is family, and being in another town should not mean we never see him.
